chapter_title: Managing Physical Disks and Partitions with Ansible
chapter_summary:
Managing physical disks and their partitions is a fundamental skill for any system administrator, and automating this with Ansible brings unparalleled efficiency and consistency. In Linux, disks are typically identified as `/dev/sda`, `/dev/sdb`, and so on. Before we can store any data, these disks need to be partitioned. Partitions define separate areas on a disk, allowing you to organize data, install multiple operating systems, or allocate space for specific purposes. Ansible's `community.general.parted` module is your primary tool for this. It provides a declarative way to manage partition tables, abstracting away the complexities of command-line tools like `parted` or `fdisk`.

When working with `parted`, you'll specify the `device` (e.g., `/dev/sdb`), the `number` of the partition, its `part_start` and `part_end` (often in MB or GB), and the `state` (e.g., `present` or `absent`). A common mistake is to forget that `parted` operates on the entire disk. If you define a partition that overlaps with an existing one, or if you attempt to create a partition on a disk that already has a partition table, you might encounter errors or, worse, unintended data loss. Always inspect the disk's current state with `lsblk` or `sudo sfdisk -l` before applying any changes. The `parted` module is designed to be idempotent; if a partition with the specified parameters (device, number, start, end) already exists, Ansible will report no changes. However, if you change the `part_end` of an existing partition, `parted` will attempt to resize it, which can be a destructive operation if not handled carefully, especially if a filesystem already exists on it.

Let's consider a practical scenario: you've added a new `/dev/sdb` disk to your server, and you need to create a single primary partition that spans the entire disk. Here's how you might do it with Ansible:

```yaml
---
- name: Configure new disk partitions
  hosts: webservers
  become: yes
  tasks:
    - name: Ensure /dev/sdb has a GPT partition table
      community.general.parted:
        device: /dev/sdb
        number: 1
        state: present
        part_start: 1MiB
        part_end: 100%
        fs_type: ext4 # This will be formatted later, but parted can set the type hint
        flags: [ 'boot' ] # Example flag, use with caution
      register: parted_result
      # This is a critical safety check. Never proceed without careful consideration.
      # In a real scenario, you might want a prompt or a very specific condition.
      when: parted_result.changed or not parted_result.changed # Always run for idempotency check

    - name: Display parted results
      ansible.builtin.debug:
        var: parted_result
```

Notice the `part_start: 1MiB` and `part_end: 100%`. Using `1MiB` for the start is a best practice to align partitions correctly, especially for modern disks and GPT partition tables. The `fs_type` parameter in `parted` primarily sets a partition type hint; it doesn't actually format the filesystem. That's a separate step we'll cover in the next chapter. For older MBR partition tables, you might specify `part_type: primary` or `part_type: logical`. Modern systems widely use GPT (GUID Partition Table), which doesn't have the primary/extended/logical distinction in the same way MBR does, allowing for many primary-like partitions. The `parted` module handles this distinction based on the partition table type it detects or creates.

**Safety Note:** Modifying partition tables is one of the most dangerous operations you can perform on a system. Always ensure you are targeting the correct device. Double-check your `device` parameter. A common mistake is to accidentally target `/dev/sda` (your OS disk) instead of `/dev/sdb` (your new data disk). This can render your system unbootable or destroy critical data. It's highly recommended to use `check_mode` (`ansible-playbook --check ...`) first to see what changes Ansible *would* make, and always have backups. If you're creating partitions on a disk that already contains data, ensure you have explicitly backed up that data, as partition table changes can make existing data inaccessible.

screens.title: Managing Physical Disks and Partitions with Ansible
screens.subtitle: Automate partition tables safely using community.general.parted

narration.text: In this lesson you'll learn how Ansible can manage physical disks and partitions using the community. general. parted module. Automated partitioning helps you provision servers consistently, avoid manual errors, and scale storage tasks across many hosts. We'll cover how to declare partitions with device names like /dev/sdb, set starts and ends using sizes or percentages, and manage part types and flags. You will see a practical playbook that creates a single primary partition spanning a new disk, and we will highlight key safety practices: starting partitions at 1MiB for alignment, verifying the target device with lsblk, and running playbooks in check mode before applying changes. You'll also learn how parted reports idempotency: if a partition matches the requested parameters, Ansible reports no change; if an end is altered, parted may resize which can be destructive. By the end of this chapter you will be able to write a guarded playbook, run it in check mode, and verify the result with lsblk or sfdisk. Think of this chapter as a careful, repeatable recipe for partitioning that reduces risk while automating routine storage setup.

keyIdea.title: Why automate partitions?
keyIdea.text: Automation ensures repeatable partition layouts, reduces human error, and scales disk setup across servers while requiring strict safety checks like check mode and device verification.

screens.title: Learning Objectives
screens.subtitle: What you'll be able to do after this chapter

narration.text: These objectives orient the practical skills you'll gain. First, you'll be able to use the community. general. parted module to declare and manage partitions programmatically. That means specifying device names, partition numbers, start and end boundaries, and requesting present or absent states so Ansible changes only what you declare. Second, you'll configure primary, extended and logical partitions when MBR is required and understand how GPT changes the model. This includes knowing when to specify part_type and when GPT makes that unnecessary. Third, you'll implement safe practices and idempotency checks: use 1MiB starts for alignment, validate the target device with lsblk or sfdisk, run the playbook in check mode to preview changes, and always have backups. Finally, you'll be able to troubleshoot common issues when automated partitioning fails, such as overlaps, mismatched partition table types, and accidental targeting of the OS disk. Each objective ties to a concrete action you can run on a VM and verify with lsblk, making the learning hands-on and verifiable.

keyIdea.title: Practical outcomes
keyIdea.text: By the end you'll write safe, idempotent playbooks that create, resize, or remove partitions while avoiding destructive mistakes.

screens.title: Why Partitions and Device Names Matter
screens.subtitle: Disks, partitions, and the /dev naming convention

narration.text: Partitions divide a physical disk into independent regions so you can organize data, host multiple filesystems, or allocate space for different services. In Linux, physical devices are identified by names such as /dev/sda and /dev/sdb. When you create the first partition on /dev/sdb, that partition becomes /dev/sdb1. Understanding that mapping is fundamental because Ansible's parted module operates on the whole device and writes partition table entries that the kernel then exposes as partition nodes. A concrete example: you add a new virtual disk to a VM and the kernel exposes it as /dev/sdb. If you create a single partition from 1MiB to 100% using parted, that zone becomes /dev/sdb1 and is available for formatting. A common misconception is that creating a partition automatically formats it; parted only sets the table and can set a type hint like ext4, but actual filesystem creation is a separate step. Another pitfall is misidentifying the device: targeting /dev/sda instead of the new /dev/sdb will modify the OS disk and can destroy the system. Always verify with lsblk or sfdisk -l to confirm device identity before running an automated playbook. How would you confirm a new disk's device name on your host right now?

keyIdea.title: Device identity is critical
keyIdea.text: Partitions are device-specific; verify the correct /dev name to avoid destructive changes to the OS disk.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 4.2 › Why partitions matter
Definition

A partition is a table entry that reserves a contiguous region on a disk. The kernel exposes these regions as separate device nodes, which you then format and mount.

Example: New disk
New disk appears as /dev/sdb. Create partition -> /dev/sdb1 becomes available for formatting.
Misconception
Creating a partition does not format it. You must run a separate mkfs step.
Key Takeaway

Confirm device identity with lsblk before altering partition tables to prevent accidental damage to the OS disk.

Quick verification commands
# List block devices and partitions
lsblk

# Show partition tables for /dev/sdb
sudo sfdisk -l /dev/sdb
Use these commands before running an Ansible playbook that modifies partitions. They are the fastest way to confirm which device is new and safe to target.

screens.title: Parameters of community.general.parted
screens.subtitle: Device, number, part_start, part_end, state, fs_type, flags

narration.text: The parted module is declarative: you describe the partition you want and Ansible applies it. The core parameters are device, which names the whole disk like /dev/sdb; number, the partition index such as 1; part_start and part_end, which accept units like MiB, GB, or percentages; and state, usually present or absent. fs_type is a partition type hint and does not format the filesystem. Flags is an array of hints, such as boot, that set partition flags. A practical example is declaring number 1, part_start 1MiB and part_end 100% to create a single partition across the disk. If you omit part_type on a GPT disk, parted will create a GPT-style partition without the primary/extended distinction. A common mistake is assuming parted will format; it won't. Another trap is specifying overlapping ranges or creating a partition on a disk with an incompatible table type. Always read the module return and test with check mode. Understanding these parameters lets you craft idempotent tasks that are clear and safe to run at scale. Parameters of community.general.parted means parted expects a declarative description of the partition; use precise parameters to let ansible make the intended changes safely.. In practical terms, device, number, part_start, part_end, state, fs_type, flags. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Describe, don't script
keyIdea.text: Parted expects a declarative description of the partition; use precise parameters to let Ansible make the intended changes safely.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 4.2 › Parted parameters
Parameter reference
  • device: absolute device path, required. Target disk is critical.
  • number: partition index, e.g. 1 for the first partition.
  • part_start / part_end: boundaries, support units such as 1MiB or percentages like 100%.
  • state: present or absent to create or remove partitions.
  • fs_type: partition type hint; does not format the partition.
  • flags: array of flags like boot for partition attributes.
Key Takeaway

Use explicit starts and ends, and treat fs_type as a hint. Always check the module return to confirm intended changes.

Concrete example
 - name: Ensure /dev/sdb has a GPT partition table
   community.general.parted:
     device: /dev/sdb
     number: 1
     state: present
     part_start: 1MiB
     part_end: 100%
     fs_type: ext4
     flags: ['boot']
   register: parted_result
This example sets a single partition spanning the whole disk. Note fs_type is only a hint; you must format the partition afterward for a usable filesystem.

screens.title: GPT versus MBR Partition Tables
screens.subtitle: When to care about primary, extended, and logical partitions

narration.text: Partition table type determines how partitions are represented and how many you can create. MBR is an older standard that limits you to four primary partitions. To work around that limit, MBR supports an extended partition that acts as a container for multiple logical partitions. By contrast, GPT is a modern standard that removes the primary versus extended distinction and allows many more partitions with a simpler model. For modern servers and virtual disks, GPT is recommended. A concrete example: on an MBR disk you might create partition 1 as primary and partition 2 as an extended container, then create /dev/sda5 and /dev/sda6 inside that extended range. On GPT, you simply add partitions 1 and 2 without container semantics. A common misconception is that 'primary' always means bootable; while primary partitions can be bootable on MBR, bootability also depends on flags and bootloaders. Another practical point is that the parted module handles the underlying table type: if you create a partition on a blank disk and specify GPT via the module, it will create a GPT table. Understanding these differences helps you choose part_type or omit it when GPT is the target format.

keyIdea.title: Choose the right table
keyIdea.text: Use GPT for modern disks; only use MBR and explicit primary/extended types when working with legacy systems that require them.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 4.2 › GPT vs MBR
GPT
Modern standard. No primary/extended split. Supports many partitions. Safer for large disks and UEFI boot setups.
Practical note: On new disks prefer GPT and start at 1MiB for alignment.
Parted behavior: You can omit part_type and parted will create GPT-style entries.
MBR
Legacy format. Up to 4 primary partitions or 3 primary plus an extended partition containing logical partitions.
Use case: Older systems or special bootloader requirements may require MBR.
Pitfall: You may need to set part_type: primary or logical explicitly when using MBR with parted.
Key Takeaway

Prefer GPT unless you have a specific legacy requirement. Know when to use part_type to meet MBR expectations.

screens.title: Safe Partitioning Workflow
screens.subtitle: Verify device, run in check mode, apply, verify again

narration.text: A safe workflow prevents accidental destruction. Start by verifying devices with lsblk or sfdisk -l to confirm you have the correct target. Next, prepare a concise playbook that targets the intended host group and device. Run ansible-playbook with --check to preview actions. Review the registered module output and planned changes carefully; if anything looks off, do not proceed. If check mode output confirms the intended plan, run the playbook for real and then re-run lsblk or sfdisk -l to confirm the partition was created with the expected start and end. If the disk contained existing data, ensure you have backups before running the playbook, because resizing or altering partition tables can make data inaccessible. A common mistake is skipping check mode or running against a broad host pattern like all. Target specific inventory hosts to limit risk. This workflow reduces surprises: verify, preview, apply, verify again. It's repeatable and can be automated into a safe provisioning pipeline with gates that require human sign-off before destructive changes. Safe Partitioning Workflow means verify the device, preview with check mode, apply the change, then verify the new partition — always have backups if data exists.. In practical terms, verify device, run in check mode, apply, verify again. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Module 4 › Chapter 4.2 › Safe workflow
Four steps

2. Prepare a focused playbook that targets a specific host or group, not all hosts.
3. Run the playbook in check mode to preview changes. Inspect the planned changes carefully.
4. If check mode is acceptable, run normally and verify results with lsblk.
Helpful commands
ansible-playbook create_partition.yml --check
ansible-playbook create_partition.yml
ansible target -m command -a "sudo lsblk"
ansible target -m command -a "sudo sfdisk -l /dev/sdb"
Common Mistake

Running the playbook without check mode or against all hosts can lead to accidental changes to the OS disk. Always scope your runs.

screens.title: Common Issues and How to Fix Them
screens.subtitle: Overlap errors, wrong device, and resizing risks

narration.text: When automating partitioning, certain failures are common and predictable. Overlap errors occur when the requested part_start and part_end intersect an existing partition; parted will refuse or report an error depending on the table. You can avoid this by first inspecting the existing partition table and by using specific ranges rather than guesses. Targeting the wrong device is a frequent and dangerous mistake—double-check the device name and use inventory scoping to avoid changing /dev/sda. Resizing existing partitions by changing part_end is risky if a filesystem already exists; resizing can lead to data loss if the filesystem isn't prepared or if the operation fails. If you must resize, ensure backups exist and use filesystem-aware tools after safely unmounting and resizing partitions. For debugging, capture the module's registered output and check the message fields for parted details. Also use lsblk and sfdisk outputs to correlate the kernel-visible state with what Ansible attempted. These steps let you diagnose whether an error is an input problem, a device selection problem, or a state-change that requires a different workflow. Common Issues and How to Fix Them means when partition tasks fail, inspect lsblk and parted_result; don't rush into formatting or resizing without backups and a clear recovery plan.. In practical terms, overlap errors, wrong device, and resizing risks. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.text: When partition tasks fail, inspect lsblk and parted_result; don't rush into formatting or resizing without backups and a clear recovery plan.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 4.2 › Troubleshooting
Common issues
  • Overlap error: Double-check start/end ranges with lsblk and sfdisk before applying.
  • Wrong device: Confirm the disk device and narrow inventory target to avoid /dev/sda mistakes.
  • Resizing risks: Avoid changing part_end on partitions with filesystems without backups and proper resize steps.
Debugging steps
Capture the module register, review parted_result.changed and parted_result.msg, and correlate with kernel output from lsblk and sfdisk. If necessary, boot into rescue mode and use backups to recover.
Tip: Run in check mode first to see what parted would change. Check mode is your safety net for catching device or range mistakes.

narration.text: part_start and part_end define the partition boundaries and accept units like MiB, GB, or percentage values such as 100%. A best practice is to start partitions at 1MiB to ensure alignment for modern disks and to avoid performance penalties or misaligned filesystems. Using 100 percent for part_end makes the partition span to the disk's end, ideal for single-partition disk setups. When you choose numeric sizes like 10GB for a specific partition, ensure the remaining space calculations leave room for other partitions if needed. A misconception is that sector-level math is required; using human-friendly units like 1MiB and 10GB is acceptable and clearer in playbooks. Be cautious when editing existing partitions: changing part_start is almost always destructive, and changing part_end may resize the partition potentially affecting the filesystem. Always document and backup before making boundary changes, and prefer creating new partitions on spare disks when possible. Understanding part_start and part_end means start partitions at 1mib to ensure proper alignment; use percentages for full-disk partitions and explicit sizes when you need reserved space.. In practical terms, units, alignment, and percentage-based ranges. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Use 1MiB start
keyIdea.text: Start partitions at 1MiB to ensure proper alignment; use percentages for full-disk partitions and explicit sizes when you need reserved space.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 4.2 › Boundary parameters
Units and examples
  • 1MiB: recommended start for alignment.
  • 10GB: explicit size for fixed partitions.
  • 100%: span to the end of the disk for single-partition designs.
Example: part_start: 1MiB and part_end: 10GB creates a partition occupying that exact range; use 100% to claim the remainder.
Risks when changing boundaries
Changing existing boundaries can require filesystem resize operations and carries risk. If a filesystem exists, resizing at the partition table level can break accessibility. Prefer new partitions or full-disk operations on blank disks.
Pro Tip

When in doubt, create a new partition on a spare disk instead of resizing a live partition with data.

screens.title: fs_type vs part_type and flags
screens.subtitle: What the module hints and what you must do separately

narration.text: fs_type and part_type are often confused. fs_type is a partition type hint that the parted module can set in the partition table; it does not create a filesystem. For example, setting fs_type to ext4 records a type hint but you still need to run a filesystem creation command such as mkfs. ext4 on the created partition. part_type applies to MBR disks to indicate primary or logical presence; on GPT disks this distinction is unnecessary and typically omitted. Flags are separate metadata like boot that set attributes important for bootloaders. A common misconception is expecting parted to both create partitions and format them in one step. Treat parted as responsible for the partition table only, and use dedicated formatting tasks afterward.
